# Third-party sources

What we reuse from other people's work: where it is from, the exact version, the licence, and which of our files use
it. This file was started with the city layer and lists only what that work uses; the earlier pins are in
`upstream/UPSTREAM_PINS.yaml` and `docs/MASTER_RESOURCE_INDEX.md` and have not been copied here yet.

| Source | Version | Licence | Paper / venue | What we use | Our files | Changed? |

### Place search (added 2026-10-06, after the per-keystroke lookups were found)

| Source | Version | Licence and terms | What we use | Our files | Changed? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Nominatim usage policy** (OSMF operations) — https://operations.osmfoundation.org/policies/nominatim/ | read 2026-10-06 | — (a usage policy, not code). Quoted: "No heavy uses (an absolute maximum of 1 request per second)"; "Provide a valid HTTP Referer or User-Agent identifying the application (stock User-Agents as set by http libraries will not do)"; "Results must be cached on your side. Clients sending repeatedly the same query may be classified as faulty and blocked"; under **Unacceptable Use**: "**Auto-complete search** This is not yet supported by Nominatim and you must not implement such a service on the client side using the API"; "Systematic queries This includes reverse queries in a grid, searching for complete lists of postcodes, towns etc." | **What the policy forbids, we no longer do:** until 2026-10-06 the From / To boxes asked Nominatim on every keystroke (an auto-complete service). Now Nominatim answers only one explicit lookup of a typed place (`resolve_place`), one reverse lookup of a point, and one city lookup, each paced at ≤ 1 per second, cached for the process, with the identifying User-Agent `traffictwin/1.0 (research, IUT Dhaka; …)` | `core/simulation/routing/trip/places.py` (`_nominatim`, `resolve_place`, `reverse_geocode`, `city_box`) | No |
| **Photon** by komoot — https://github.com/komoot/photon ; public API https://photon.komoot.io/ | public API as read 2026-10-06 (the server's version is not published; the software's latest release at reading was the 1.x line; data: OpenStreetMap) | Software Apache-2.0 ("photon is open source and licensed under Apache License, Version 2.0"); data ODbL © OpenStreetMap contributors. Public API terms, quoted from photon.komoot.io: "You can use the API for your project, but please be fair - extensive usage will be throttled. We do not guarantee for the availability and usage might be subject of change in the future." Its stated purpose is "search as you type with OpenStreetMap" | **Suggestions as someone types** (the only geocoder asked for them): `GET /api/?q=&bbox=w,s,e,n&limit=&lang=en`, bounded to the city's box. Fair use on our side: the browser waits for a pause in typing (400 ms), asks only from 3 characters, never for a `lat, lng` pair, at most once a second, and cancels a lookup newer text made stale; the backend paces to ≤ 1 request per second per process, caches every answer, and sends the identifying User-Agent. If Photon is silent there are no suggestions (never a fall-back to Nominatim). A self-hosted Photon or Amazon Location Places would be the step up if the public API ever throttles us | `core/simulation/routing/trip/places.py` (`_photon`, `suggest`), `frontend/src/lib/places.ts` (`usePlaceSuggestions`), `backend/tests/routing/test_places_suggest.py`, `frontend/src/lib/places.test.ts` | No (a separate service, used through its HTTP API) |

### Ambulance reach, nearest hospitals, map matching (added 2026-10-06, queue item 1)

| Source | Version | Licence and terms | What we use | Our files | Changed? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Valhalla web app** by GIS•OPS — https://github.com/gis-ops/valhalla-app | HEAD `439ea98f184f8821a7e9146a48af1f383a40ce05` (master, read 2026-10-06) | MIT ("MIT License, Copyright (c) 2022 GIS • OPS UG") | **The request shape and the colours, no code copied:** `src/utils/valhalla.ts` `buildIsochronesRequest` / `makeContours` (`polygons: true, denoise, generalize, contours: [{time}]`) is what our backend sends to our own server; `src/utils/isochrone-palettes.ts` "blues" (`#084594 #4292c6 #9ecae1`) colours our 10/20/30-minute contours. The app itself implements directions and isochrones; the matrix and map matching below are the engine's own APIs, not the app's | `core/simulation/routing/valhalla.py` (`isochrone`), `frontend/src/features/emergency/reach.ts` (`BLUES`) | No |
| **Valhalla** engine APIs `/isochrone`, `/sources_to_targets`, `/trace_attributes` (the server already in "Whole-city routing") | 3.9.0 | MIT | Isochrone polygons around a hospital; the time matrix hospital → grid point (the server refuses more than 2 500 source×target pairs per call, so calls are sliced); map matching of opted-in phone fixes (`shape_match: map_snap`, the OpenStreetMap way id and the metres each fix moved). The recorded-speed reach is **our own method** on top of the matrix: a path from hospital H to point T passes a recorded site S when t(H,S)+t(S,T) ≤ t(H,T)+30 s, and then S's measured stretch is re-timed with the recorded median speed (the same rule as the whole-city routes) — stated in the Research table | `core/simulation/routing/valhalla.py` (`matrix`, `trace`), `core/safety/reach.py`, `backend/app/probes/snap.py` (`ValhallaSnap`) | No |
| **OpenStreetMap hospitals** through the Overpass API — https://overpass-api.de/ ; mirrors as in `backend/app/transit/osm.py` | data as of `osm3s.timestamp_osm_base` recorded in the file (Dhaka: 2026-10-06T14:33:00Z, 477 elements, 37 tagged `emergency=yes`) | ODbL, © OpenStreetMap contributors; Overpass guidance quoted in "Add your city" | One query per city, `amenity=hospital` nodes/ways/relations with `out center`, kept in `data/cities/<city>/hospitals.json` with the query, the instance that answered, the date and a sha256 of the list; never re-asked while the file exists. For Dhaka the main instance was unreachable on 2026-10-06 (~14:40 UTC); the same query was run once by hand on the mail.ru mirror and the file records that | `core/safety/hospitals.py`, `data/cities/dhaka/hospitals.json`, `evidence/reach/dhaka/hospitals.json` | No |

### Crash SOS (added 2026-10-06, queue item Q2)

| **WreckWatch** — Jules White, Chris Thompson, Hamilton Turner, Brian Dougherty, Douglas C. Schmidt, "WreckWatch: Automatic Traffic Accident Detection and Notification with Smartphones", *Mobile Networks and Applications* 16(3), 2011; author copy https://www.dre.vanderbilt.edu/~schmidt/PDF/wreckwatch.pdf | journal version, 2011 (read 2026-10-06) | A paper (Springer); read for its rule, nothing copied | **The detection rule:** "ignores any acceleration events below 4G's, a value designed to detect even minor accidents but filter out a drop or sudden stop", and an alarm only "when a GPS sensor indicates that the smartphone is moving faster than 15 miles per hour and when the recorded acceleration exceeds 4G". We apply the 4 g threshold to the magnitude of `accelerationIncludingGravity`; the speed floor only when a speed is known, and we say when it was not applied. WreckWatch's second signal (a loud acoustic event) is **not** implemented | `core/safety/sos.py`, `frontend/src/features/emergency/sos.ts` | No |
| **DeviceMotion API** — W3C "DeviceOrientation Event Specification", MDN https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/DeviceMotionEvent | as read 2026-10-06 | Web platform API (W3C; MDN docs CC-BY-SA) | `devicemotion` events, `accelerationIncludingGravity` (m/s²); `DeviceMotionEvent.requestPermission()` on iOS; `navigator.onLine` / `online`/`offline` events and `navigator.connection.effectiveType` (where present) choose the path; `navigator.vibrate` on detection | `frontend/src/features/emergency/useMotion.ts`, `SosCard.tsx` | — |

They show what the rule does; they are not recordings and say nothing about how often real crashes or false alarms occur | `research/sos/traces/*.json` + `SHA256SUMS`, `evidence/sos/results.json` | — |
| The offline leg's numbers | — | — | From the city's own saved mesh result (`core/networking/mesh/results.py`, SIMULATED, PONS; already in this file under "Offline mesh"), the same `plain` the Offline alerts page states | `core/safety/sos.py` `path_steps` | No |

### Works with weak signal (added 2026-10-06, queue item Q3; main references changed by the owner the same evening)

| Source | Version | Licence and terms | What we use | Our files | Changed? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Bartendr** — Aaron Schulman, Vishnu Navda, Ramachandran Ramjee, Neil Spring, "Bartendr: A Practical Approach to Energy-aware Cellular Data Scheduling", ACM MobiCom 2010. PDF https://www.cs.albany.edu/~mariya/courses/csi525S18/papers/mobicom10-bartendr.pdf | read 2026-10-06; local copy `papers/bartendr_mobicom2010.pdf`, sha256 `1ddd1d9309472fcf5877d14f39dbe6d2b4bb08ae6167246e89e39a4e0ba0f165` | A paper (© ACM); read for its method and measured numbers, no code exists or is copied; the PDF is kept for the owner's reading only, not redistributed | **Main reference.** (1) Predict along a known track, not from location alone: "the pattern of variation in signal strength is quite stable when location is coupled with direction of travel. Bartendr, thus, leverages the notion of a track, e.g., the route from a user's home to workplace"; tracks are kept per direction ("Tracks from opposite directions may not align in signal strength"); 100 m steps. Our track is the chosen route, and our history cells are already per heading octant. (2) Energy per bit: "the overall energy required to transfer a fixed chunk of data, i.e. energy per bit, can be as much as six times higher (25% throughput and 50% more power)" on poor signal; "communicating at -90 instead of at -70 RSSI entails the use of about 20% additional power ... and a median throughput that is 50% lower ... an energy per bit on the Pre that is 2.4 times higher". Palm Pre power anchors (Fig. 7 text): baseline "400 mW", data "around 1500 mW", tail until about 3 s after the transfer. (3) Scheduling: a threshold for syncs ("-75 RSSI") and, for a stream of chunks, "a dynamic programming formulation that computes the minimum energy schedule" counting tail energy, because "a greedy approach that ignores the radio tail behavior can be very inefficient". We use (2) only as a **labelled estimate** ("estimated from Bartendr's Palm Pre measurements, not measured on our phones"), with throughput per level kept at the paper's measured ratios (strong = our fast-4G preset, medium 1/2, weak 1/4) and (3)'s dynamic programme for the pack download | `core/simulation/routing/signal.py`, `frontend/src/lib/schedule.ts`, `frontend/tests/weak_signal.experiment.cjs` | — |
| **BreadCrumbs** — Anthony J. Nicholson, Brian D. Noble, "BreadCrumbs: Forecasting Mobile Connectivity", ACM MobiCom 2008. PDF https://web.eecs.umich.edu/~bnoble/UM_EECS/Current_Research_files/p46-nicholson.pdf | read 2026-10-06; local copy `papers/breadcrumbs_mobicom2008.pdf`, sha256 `de8aa5560d2e3d5e4dac6d093b070f936ac7ca74f3703d5ee6b4a1ebdd1ee125` | A paper (© ACM); method only, nothing copied | **Main reference** for the personal forecast. A per-person mobility model on the device: "a second-order Markov model, each state consists of two sets of coordinates: the location where the device was during the last state, and its current location", useful "for distinguishing between ... eastbound and westbound on the same street"; positions rounded "to three decimal places" (a 0.001° grid); a state transition every τ = 10 s; "a second-order Markov model, with fallback to a first-order model when the second-order model has no prediction"; the forecast is "the weighted sum ... of the best bandwidth previously seen ... weighted by the transition probability", recursive for more steps. Training: "sufficiently accurate, even with as little as one week of training" (next-step bandwidth "within 50 KB/s for over 80% of the time"). Our version keeps the model and the readings **only in the browser's storage** (nothing leaves the phone) and is used for a saved trip only after **5 completed trips** of it (our reading of "one week" of weekday commutes; the page shows "learning: n of 5") | `frontend/src/lib/breadcrumbs.ts` | — |
| **Prediction-based prefetch** — M. Borkowski, O. Skarlat, S. Schulte, S. Dustdar, "Prediction-Based Prefetch Scheduling in Mobile Service Applications", IEEE MS 2016, pp. 41–48, DOI 10.1109/MobServ.2016.17 | abstract only (the full text is not open) | — | **Secondary citation:** "a prefetch scheduling algorithm based on network quality predictions ... can improve the user-perceived response time by up to 95 %" — the idea of fetching before a predicted-poor stretch | — | — |
| **Planetiler** — https://github.com/onthegomap/planetiler | release v0.10.2 (latest on 2026-10-06); the jar's sha256 and each output's hash recorded in `evidence/tiles/TILES_BASEMAP.txt` at build time | Apache-2.0 | Builds our OpenMapTiles-schema vector tiles for Dhaka and Los Angeles from the same Geofabrik extracts as Valhalla, one PMTiles file per city in the routing bucket | `infra/tiles/build.sh` | No |
| **OpenFreeMap "liberty" style** — https://github.com/hyperknot/openfreemap-styles `styles/liberty/style.json`, sprite `sprites/sprites/ofm_f384/` | main at `cf9e8e728d704b5659d22dc2aebb4053bfbbb30e` (read 2026-10-06) | Repository MIT; the style JSON BSD-3-Clause ("derived from OSM Bright from Mapbox Open Styles ... retains the same BSD license", `styles/liberty/LICENSE.md`, copied to `frontend/public/liberty/LICENSE.md`); OpenMapTiles schema design CC BY 4.0 | Our own style for the trip pack: the same layers over **our** tiles; remote references replaced by ours (`infra/tiles/make_style.py`); the Natural Earth raster source dropped. OpenFreeMap's tile service stays for normal viewing and is never prefetched | `frontend/public/liberty/` | Yes: sources, sprite and glyph URLs only |
| **Noto Sans glyphs** — https://github.com/maplibre/demotiles `font/` | gh-pages, read 2026-10-06; ranges 768–1023 and 7680–7935 added 2026-10-10 from gh-pages commit `601ae60796ceceda2cbd2ed3d2ea92d17a84be4b` (the existing `Noto Sans Regular/0-255.pbf` is byte-identical at that commit) | Repository BSD-3-Clause; Noto Sans under the SIL Open Font License 1.1 | Regular, Italic, Bold, ranges 0–255, 256–511, 768–1023 (combining marks), 2304–2559 (Bengali), 7680–7935 (Latin Extended Additional), 8192–8447, served from this app; the two added ranges because labels in our Dhaka tiles use them (their 404s seen offline, `evidence/offline_home/`) | `frontend/public/fonts/` | No |

| Source | Version | Licence and terms | What we use | Our files | Changed? |

| **Ferrostar** by Stadia Maps — https://github.com/stadiamaps/ferrostar | HEAD `4e2d7f647952c0a4060efd584e6edfc6148092b9` (read 2026-10-07); npm `@stadiamaps/ferrostar-webcomponents@0.57.0` and `@stadiamaps/ferrostar@0.57.0` (its Rust core compiled to WebAssembly) | BSD-3-Clause (`LICENSE.txt`, "Copyright (c) 2023, Stadia Maps, Inc.") | The web components unchanged: `FerrostarCore` (Valhalla request in its own OSRM format with banner and voice instructions, the navigation session: snapping, step advance, off-route recalculation), `FerrostarMap` linked to our own Home map (route, puck, instruction banner), `SimulatedLocationProvider` (the demo drive, ×8 speed, said on screen) and `BrowserLocationProvider`. ### Design lineage of the forecast-routing loop (recorded 2026-10-12, owner's request)

| Source | Version | Licence | Paper / venue | What we use | Our files | Changed? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **PRE-VE** — Santamaria, A. F., Fazio, P., Raimondo, P., Tropea, M., De Rango, F., "A New Distributed Predictive Congestion Aware Re-Routing Algorithm for CO2 Emissions Reduction", IEEE Transactions on Vehicular Technology 68(5), May 2019, pp. 4419-4433, doi:10.1109/TVT.2019.2905753 (the owner refers to it as "PRE-VE"; that label was not found in the paper's metadata, 2026-10-12 web check) | the paper (no code released) | — | IEEE TVT 2019 | **Design comparison only.** Our RQ2 loop (forecast → road prices → alternatives → a reroute message over a simulated link → `setRoute`) is comparable to PRE-VE's predictive, congestion-aware rerouting over 802.11p in Veins/SUMO. No code copied (none is public). Ours differs: Graph WaveNet trained on METR-LA plus a residual correction from the cars' status reports as the forecaster; duarouter alternatives with a 60 s / 5 % saving threshold, cooldown, share and capacity admission (BPR) as the decision rules; a latency / loss / lifetime channel on infrastructure as the link. Demand is synthetic (randomTrips, 8x peak), the map and the METR-LA speeds are real | `features/forecast-routing/README.md` (Design lineage) | — |
